# Incident Report: DESKTOP-ES9F3ML Compromise — 2026-01-31

## 1. Victim Host

| Attribute | Value |
|---|---|
| IPv4 address | **10.1.21.58** |
| MAC address | **00:21:5d:c8:0e:f2** |
| Windows hostname | **DESKTOP-ES9F3ML** (also broadcasting NetBIOS alias `WIN11OFFICE`) |
| Logged-in Windows user | **gwyatt** (recovered from Kerberos `CNameString`) |
| Gateway/LAN | 10.1.21.2/24 (DHCP server 10.1.21.1, MAC 00:04:c1:be:8c:d4) |

## 2. Malware Family and Attribution

**Behavioral attribution only — not signature-confirmed.** No IDS/Suricata alert export was present in the evidence folder (only the pcap itself), and the payload transfer was carried over TLS, so no file could be carved out and hashed from the capture. I am not naming a specific malware family with confidence, because doing so would require a hash/YARA/threat-intel match I cannot produce from packet data alone.

What the traffic *does* show, behaviorally, is a classic fake-download / "ClickFix"-style delivery chain into a commodity Windows stealer/loader:

1. **hiyter.com** (104.21.22.231) — initial redirector, contacted at T+45.35s.
2. **media.megafilehub4.lat** (104.21.48.156) — fake file-hosting landing page, T+45.92s.
3. **cdnjs.cloudflare.com** — legitimate CDN library pulled in by the lure page (fingerprinting/obfuscation script), T+47.8s.
4. **arch.filemegahab4.sbs** (104.21.46.67) — payload delivery host. A single ~16 MB HTTPS transfer runs from T+48.36s to T+70.75s (22.4s), consistent with a padded stealer/loader installer being downloaded and executed.
5. **whooptm.cyou** (62.72.32.156) — post-execution check-in, T+90.37s.
6. **whitepepper.su** (153.92.1.49) — C2/gate server. Confirmed via cleartext HTTP:
   - `GET /api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&agent=Chrome` → returns a JS browser-fingerprinting stub (collects `navigator.*`, WebGL vendor/renderer, hardware concurrency, etc.)
   - `POST /api/set_agent?...&act=log` → exfiltrates the collected fingerprint (platform Win32, Chrome/144, AMD Radeon R9 200 series GPU, 12 logical cores) back to the server.
   - This same id/token pair was replayed with `agent=Edge`, indicating the malware profiled multiple installed browsers.
   - Traffic to this host is a sustained beacon: 24 TCP connections (18 on 443, 6 on 80) between T+92s and T+122s — persistent C2 check-in behavior, not a one-off request.
7. **holiday-forever.cc** (80.97.160.24, T+122.8s) and **communicationfirewall-security.cc** (104.21.9.36 / 172.67.141.109, T+126.5s) — additional suspicious TLS-only contacts in the same post-infection window, likely secondary C2/redirect infrastructure (role not fully resolvable — TLS-encrypted, no cleartext HTTP observed to these hosts).

No file names or SHA256 hashes could be grounded in evidence: every payload-carrying transfer identified above is TLS-encrypted and no TLS key log was supplied, so tshark cannot recover the object. Do not treat any hash you may see elsewhere for this activity as confirmed by this capture.

## 3. Indicators of Compromise (all observed directly in the pcap)

**Malicious domains:**
- `hiyter.com`
- `media.megafilehub4.lat`
- `arch.filemegahab4.sbs`
- `whooptm.cyou`
- `whitepepper.su`
- `holiday-forever.cc`
- `communicationfirewall-security.cc`

**C2 / malicious endpoints (IP:port):**
- `153.92.1.49:443` and `153.92.1.49:80` — whitepepper.su, active C2/fingerprint-exfil beacon
- `104.21.46.67:443` — arch.filemegahab4.sbs, payload delivery (Cloudflare-fronted)
- `104.21.48.156:443` — media.megafilehub4.lat, lure/landing page (Cloudflare-fronted)
- `62.72.32.156:443` — whooptm.cyou
- `80.97.160.24:443` — holiday-forever.cc
- `104.21.9.36:443` / `172.67.141.109` — communicationfirewall-security.cc
- `104.21.22.231:443` — hiyter.com

**Malicious URLs (full, observed in cleartext HTTP):**
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge`
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Chrome&act=log` (POST, exfil)
- `http://whitepepper.su/api/set_agent?id=3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C&token=842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b&description=&agent=Edge&act=log` (POST, exfil)

**Unique bot/session identifier:** `3BF67EC05320C5729578BE4C0ADF174C` (id) / `842e2802df0f0a06b4ed51f12f4387e761523b` (token) — this pair keys the victim's session on the whitepepper.su C2 panel.

**Transferred files/hashes:** None recoverable. The ~16 MB payload transfer to arch.filemegahab4.sbs (104.21.46.67, T+48.36s–70.75s) is the most likely malware drop point by size and timing, but it is TLS-encrypted end-to-end in this capture — no filename, Content-Disposition, or hash is available without TLS decryption keys, which were not provided.

## 4. Recommended Next Steps
- Isolate 10.1.21.58 (DESKTOP-ES9F3ML) from the network immediately if not already done.
- Block the domains/IPs listed above at DNS/proxy/firewall.
- Acquire disk/memory image of the host to identify the actual dropped binary and compute its SHA256 for definitive family attribution (current attribution is behavioral only).
- Rotate credentials for user **gwyatt** and any accounts/browser-saved credentials on that machine, given the C2 exhibited stealer-style browser fingerprinting/exfil behavior.
